content:
The image shows a soybean stem split lengthwise, revealing the internal tissue. Key observations:

- The stem has been cut open longitudinally
- The pith and vascular tissue are clearly **dark brown to chocolate-brown** throughout the interior
- The external stem surface appears relatively normal/pale (no obvious external cankers or lesions)
- The browning is concentrated in the pith and vascular tissue, especially visible as a continuous brown discoloration running through the stem

Reasoning through the candidates:

- **Brown Stem Rot**: Classic diagnostic feature is brown pith and vascular tissue when stem is split lengthwise, especially at nodes. External stem looks healthy. This matches perfectly.
- **Sudden Death Syndrome**: Would show *white* pith when stems are cut — clearly not the case here.
- **Phytophthora**: Shows chocolate-brown discoloration extending from soil line upward on the *outside* of the stem; internal tissue is also discolored but the external presentation is distinct.
- **Fusarium**: Brown vascular tissue in roots/stems but typically accompanied by external foliar symptoms and root rot.

The image is a textbook demonstration of Brown Stem Rot — split stem with brown pith/vascular tissue, externally healthy-looking stem. This is the key diagnostic feature specifically called out in the BSR description: "Healthy stems have white pith, while BSR-infected stems have brown pith."
